`.pi` files as modules, with HMR, dependency tracking (through
`piton compile --dependencies`) and virtual modules. Each export in the Piton
file is a named export, and the default export is the whole file, the same as
`piton compile` gives:

```ts
import { SaveButton } from '../spec/app.pi';
import spec from '../spec/app.pi';

const button = SaveButton;
const cancel = spec.CancelButton;
```

It has a configurable default renderer (`renderer: 'json' | 'yaml' |
'markdown'`), and the renderers can also be imported as functions
(`vite-plugin-piton/renderers`) and used inline. `packages/astro-piton` is an
Astro integration that wraps the Vite plugin.

## 15. Working on a specbase

1. **Orient.** Open `piton.config.pi` to find `root`, `entry`, `output`, the
   frameworks, the adapters, `codeRoot` and `shapeRoot`. Read the entry file,
   usually `spec/index.pi`, because its exports are the compilation roots.
   Follow the `index.pi` files down through the modules. In this repository,
   `spec/index.pi` exports `Specification` (FoundingThesis, Language, Tooling,
   Belay, PackageManagement) plus the skills and command in `spec/agent/`.
2. **Read compiled reference for overview, and source for truth.**
   `<referenceRoot>/**/*.md` is easy to browse, and its links are lazy, so
   follow them only when relevant.
3. **Edit the `.pi` source**, following the conventions around it:
   - one exported anchor per file, named after the file;
   - `index.pi` files that re-export with `from ./X export *`;
   - abstract anchors exported with a keyword, and shared abstracts in a
     `lib/` folder;
   - lowerCamelCase property names;
   - SCREAMING_CASE for exported constant lists;
   - prose in string blocks, and structure in keys and lists;
   - `@{X}` to link related documents;
   - examples inside fences wrapped in a `\\\` escape block.
4. **Keep imports honest.** Use `use` for keywords and `from ... import` for
   names; a file often needs both. A new file only compiles if the entry
   reaches it, so export it through an index or reference it.
5. **Validate.**
   - Run `piton check`.
   - `piton check` does **not** compile the examples inside escape blocks
     (they are literal text). When you edit spec examples, extract each ` ```piton ` block,
     run `piton compile` on it, and compare with any ` ```json ` block that

use /ui

    concept: {ScrollbarConcept}

concept ScrollbarConcept:
    pitch:
        A permanent scrollbar for any list that scrolls, laid out as a narrow
        column of its own beside the list rather than over it.

    shape: {ScrollbarShape}

shape ScrollbarShape:
    description:
        A narrow column along the right of the list, always shown, whether or not the list has anything to scroll. It
        is the list's only scrollbar: no scrollbar is laid over the list, or
        appears only while hovering or scrolling.

    surface:
        Every scrollbar is this one, wherever it is. It has no background of
        its own: the column takes the colour of the surface it sits on, so on
        the file tree it is the tree's colour, and on a panel's body the
        body's. Nothing in it is a colour of its own; the track, the thumb's
        ends, the arrows, and the thumb's lightening are all black or white
        laid over that surface, so the scrollbar looks the same on any of
        them.

        The strengths given here are dark mode's. Light mode takes the same
        steps, gentler: the track is black laid a fifth of the way over the
        surface, the thumb's ends a tenth, and the thumb lightens with white
        laid about a fifth of the way while hovered and about a third while
        dragged. Its arrows are darker than the surface rather than lighter,
        black laid about a third of the way over it, since white would all but
        vanish on a light surface.

    buttons:
        A square button at the top of the column scrolls the list up a little,
        and a square button at the bottom scrolls it down a little. The column
        is 18 pixels wide, and each button is 17 pixels tall, as wide as the
        column. A button shows only a small solid arrow, pointing up or down,
        6 pixels wide and 4 tall, centred across it, 7 pixels from its top
        pointing up and from its bottom pointing down, drawn crisp on whole
        pixels rather than smoothed, in a faint grey, #4d4d4d on #222222 in
        dark mode, white laid about a fifth of the way over the surface; it
        has no background, border, or line of its own until the
        pointer is over it, when it has the bevel of the @{ThemeScope}, and
        while pressed with the pointer still over it, its pressed bevel
        instead. Neither bevel takes the mouse.

    track:
        Between the buttons runs the track, from just beneath the top button
        to just above the bottom one, inset one pixel from either side of the
        column, so a pixel of the surface shows down both its sides. The track
        is dark, black laid half way over the surface, #111111 on #222222 in
        dark mode, and no line runs beside it or around it. The column has no
        border at all, against the list or anywhere else.

        The track holds a thumb as tall as the share of the list in view, and
        never too short to grab, placed as far down the track as the list is
        scrolled. The thumb is a plain rectangle, as wide as the column,
        covering the track's inset, with no rounded corners, no border, no
        bevel, and no background of its own: it is the surface's colour, so it
        reads as a gap of the surface in the dark track. Its top and bottom
        ends each have a single pixel between the track's colour and the
        surface's, black laid a quarter of the way over the surface, #191919
        on #222222 in dark mode, softening where the track meets it. It
        lightens a step while the pointer is over it, as white laid over it,
        and another step while it is being dragged, white laid about 3.5% and
        7% of the way over it in dark mode, and goes back as soon as neither
        is true. Nothing in the column lightens while something else, like a
        sidebar's edge, is being dragged across it. With nothing to scroll, the
        thumb fills the track.

        Pressing the thumb and dragging scrolls the list with it for as long as
        the button is held, even once the pointer leaves the column, and
        pressing the track elsewhere moves the thumb there, from where it can
        be dragged straight away. Where a resize edge beside the list overlaps
        the column, a press goes to whichever of the two has the smaller hit
        area, as the main window says.

    steadiness:
        The thumb never jumps. Its size and place always reflect the whole
        list's real height, including a list that only draws the rows in view:
        every row is measured, even those never scrolled into view, so the
        thumb doesn't grow, shrink, or leap as rows come into view. A row that
        arrives, or changes, while out of view counts at its height as soon as
        it does, and after the list's width changes, rewrapping its rows, the
        height is known in full again by the next frame. Only what has changed
        is measured again, so a long list stays as quick to scroll and to add to
        as one that measures only what is in view; only a change of width
        measures every row again.

        A row's height is the same measured out of view as drawn in it. Text in
        a row, such as a reply's markdown, is parsed once and kept for as long
        as the app runs, not only while its row is drawn, so a row scrolled
        away and back is never parsed again, nor shorter for a moment while it
        is. Long text is parsed in the background, so a row holding it may
        first measure short: while it parses, its row is measured again every
        fraction of a second, for a few seconds at most, so the height is right
        as soon as the parse lands, whether or not the row is in view. Dragging
        the thumb, it stays under the pointer the whole way, rows coming into
        view or not.

    lockToBottom:
        A list that keeps receiving output, like a task's, adds one more square
        button, drawn as the others are, below the others, with a pixel of the
        surface between it and the down button, that locks the scroll to the
        bottom. Its arrow is the down arrow with a short bar beneath it, the
        same 6 pixels wide. While it is locked, the button shows as selected,
        with the pressed bevel of the @{ThemeScope} whether or not the pointer
        is over it, and the list stays scrolled to the bottom as output
        arrives. Pressing it again unlocks it. Its tooltip says
        which it will do.

            the lock button once, to confirm it. It is a single, brief

            of it is over in under a second. It is drawn over whatever is beside
            the column, but never takes the mouse.

            scroll while it pulses stops the pulse straight away.

        the mouse wheel or trackpad over the list, pressing the column's up or
        down button, or pressing or dragging its thumb. Scrolled by hand to the
        bottom, the scroll locks there, just as if the button had been pressed.

        breaks straight away, leaving the list wherever it was scrolled to. A

        the way to lock or unlock it wherever the list is: pressing it to lock
        scrolls the list to the bottom, and pressing it to unlock leaves the
        list unlocked until it is next scrolled to the bottom by hand.

        A surface that should lift slightly off what it sits on, such as a
        table's header or a hovered scrollbar button, can have the theme's bevel: a
        very slight 1 pixel edge around it, just enough to lift it. Its top and
        left edges are a touch lighter, as white laid faintly over the surface,
        8% in dark mode and 55% in light mode; its bottom and right edges only
        barely darker, as black laid very faintly over it, 6% in dark mode and

        line. Laid over rather than a colour of its own, it looks the same on
        any surface, hovered, pressed, or tinted. The lit top runs the full
        width, and the lit left side runs beneath it; the shaded bottom runs the
        full width, and the shaded right side runs above it, so no two edges
        overlap. It sits inside the surface, taking no room, and isn't a border
        in the sense of lines never being doubled.

        A surface being pressed in can have the bevel pressed instead: the same
        edges, with the light and shade swapped, so its top and left edges are
